title: Finding and Nurturing American’s Next Top Math Stars
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman interviews Ilana Walder-Biesanz, founder and CEO of National Math Stars, a nonprofit that identifies mathematically exceptional children around third grade and supports them over the long term. The programme gives awards to top scorers, invites their families to apply for wraparound support, places them in courses matched to their level through providers such as Art of Problem Solving, and funds enrichment on a sliding scale by family need. Aldeman presses her on the obvious objections, why gifted children need help and what districts gain, and she answers with both a fairness argument and evidence from the Study of Mathematically Precocious Youth and the Lost Einsteins research. She explains the state partnership model, in which a state such as Iowa uses its own test data to find top scorers so that rural and lower-income children are not missed, while keeping student data private. The programme is only three and a half years old, operates in ten states, and she is open that evidence for supporting older students is still thin.
points: Children far ahead in maths rarely get a structured intervention, whereas those far behind do; National Math Stars aims to fill that gap.
Universal screening through state test data finds talented children in rural and lower-income districts that school-by-school outreach misses.
Support is placed by mathematical level rather than age, mostly out of school, so districts do not need to change anything to benefit.
Need-based funding aims to stop family income from determining who gets the enrichment that predicts later scientific achievement.
The founder admits her model is well tested for grades 3 to 6 but unproven for middle and high school students.
quotes: I recently had a chance to meet Ilana Walder-Biesanz, the Founder and CEO of National Math Stars. She is on a mission to identify and support the mathematical abilities of extraordinary young students.

Along with the medals, a letter goes home to their parents, telling them that their child is probably ready for a lot more. The letter gives them resources they can use immediately, and it also invites them to apply to a longer-term wraparound support program.

And we really try to take cues from an individual kid’s interest. We’re trying to connect them to coding clubs, robotics clubs, biochemistry classes, astronomy classes — anything in STEM that aligns to their interest.
When a student is very far ahead, most schools don’t have much in the way of interventions in place to make sure that they can still be learning and growing, and that’s the gap that we are filling.

Now, if we work with the district to accelerate a kid, yes, that may introduce logistical challenges, but one that’s only one option. We love it when districts are willing to work with us to make that happen and to make those hours in school be more productive.
We had thought before about working at the state level, but this was the first time we actually had the opportunity to do it.
We have the funding capacity and the team capacity and the appetite to expand, and we’re working towards a truly national footprint.
